title: What a Dental Abscess Feels Like and Why It Needs Urgent Care
metaTitle: Dental Abscess Symptoms and When It's Urgent
metaDescription: Learn what a dental abscess feels like, the warning signs that make it urgent, and when to seek emergency dental care in Markham. Clear, practical guidance.
secondaryKeywords: what does a dental abscess feel like
excerpt: A dental abscess usually causes throbbing pain, swelling, and a bad taste from draining pus - and it typically needs prompt care. Here is how to recognize one and when it becomes an emergency.
heroImageAlt: A person holding their swollen cheek in discomfort, suggesting a possible dental abscess.
bodyHtml:
A dental abscess usually feels like a persistent, throbbing toothache that can be severe, often with swelling in the gum, cheek, or jaw, a bad taste from draining pus, tenderness when you bite, and sometimes fever. The short answer to whether it is an emergency is: yes, in most cases it needs prompt dental care. An abscess is a pocket of pus caused by a bacterial infection, and it will not reliably clear on its own. When swelling spreads quickly, affects your eye or neck, or makes it hard to breathe or swallow, that is a medical emergency and you should seek urgent care right away.

What a dental abscess actually feels like

People describe an abscess in different ways, but a few experiences come up again and again. The pain is often constant rather than fleeting, and it may pulse or throb in time with your heartbeat. It can radiate to the ear, jaw, or neck on the same side, and it frequently worsens when you lie down. The affected tooth may feel slightly raised or loose, and biting on it can be sharply uncomfortable.

Swelling is a common companion. You might notice a puffy area along the gum, a swollen cheek, or tenderness under the jaw. Some people feel a small bump on the gum that leaks a salty or foul-tasting fluid; this is often a sign that the infection has found a path to drain. If that bump appears and the pain suddenly eases, the infection has not gone away. It has simply released some pressure.

Why an abscess needs timely attention

An abscess is your body walling off a bacterial infection, often from a tooth whose inner pulp has died or from deep gum disease. Because the source of the infection remains, the problem tends to persist or return until a dentist addresses it. Antibiotics may reduce swelling and buy time, but on their own they are not a cure. Definitive treatment usually means draining the infection and removing its source, which is why your dentist may discuss root canal treatment to save the tooth or, in some situations, extraction.

Left untreated, infection can spread into surrounding bone and soft tissue. Serious spread is uncommon when people seek care promptly, but it can become dangerous, which is exactly why dentists and organizations such as the Canadian Dental Association treat facial swelling from a dental infection as something to act on rather than wait out.

When is a dental abscess a true emergency?

Call for urgent or emergency care if you have rapidly spreading swelling, swelling that reaches your eye or closes it, difficulty swallowing or breathing, a high fever with chills, or a generally unwell feeling alongside facial swelling. These signal that the infection may be moving beyond the tooth. If breathing or swallowing is affected, go to a hospital emergency department.

What can I do before I am seen?

While you arrange care, gentle measures can help you cope: rinsing with warm salt water, keeping your head elevated when resting, and using over-the-counter pain relief as directed on the label and appropriate for your health. Avoid placing aspirin directly on the gum, and do not try to pop or squeeze a gum bump. These steps manage symptoms; they do not treat the underlying infection.

Will the pain going away mean it is healed?

Not necessarily. Pain can fade when an abscess drains or when the nerve inside a tooth dies completely, yet the infection often remains active. A tooth that stopped hurting can still need treatment, so it is worth having it assessed even if you feel better.

Getting help in Markham

If you are dealing with swelling, throbbing pain, or a gum bump that keeps returning, it is reasonable to seek care promptly rather than hope it settles. Dr. Neda Kadivar is a general and family dentist with over 20 years of experience who provides root canal treatment at her Markham practice, and her team can help you understand whether an abscess is the cause and what the options are. You can learn more about the practice through Smile Dental Arts Centre in Markham, and if you think you may have a dental emergency, their dental emergencies page explains how urgent situations are handled. For anyone across the Greater Toronto Area, including North York residents considering care in Markham, acting early usually keeps a treatable problem from becoming a bigger one.

An abscess is a clear signal from your body that something needs attention. Recognizing the signs, taking sensible comfort measures, and reaching out to a dentist quickly are the steps most likely to protect both your tooth and your overall health.

This article is general information and not a substitute for professional dental advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always speak with a licensed dentist about your specific situation.
